newsitem.title: UK: Chances high of UK policy error-leading economist.
newsitem.headline: Chances high of UK policy error-leading economist.

text.p: The chances of making a major monetary policy error in Britain are much greater now than in 1987, when the British economy was similarly poised, a leading economist said on Monday.

But Gavyn Davies, chief economist at Goldman Sachs and tipped to become the next Governor or deputy governor of the Bank of England, told the House of Commons Treasury select committee he was still a reluctant disciple in favour of further interest rate rises.

"If sterling stays at the levels it is at currently and if the government sticks to its spending plans -- both very big 'ifs' -- the Bank is already risking overkill," he told the House of Commons Treasury select committee.
"Without those two conditions in place, interest rates almost certainly need to rise in the future and should have done so already."
He said there was no need for a significant monetary tightening, only gradual rate rises until there was evidence of a decline in consumer confidence and in leading indicators of inflation.

Davies and three other leading economists were testifying to the committee on budgetary and monetary issues in a warm up to appearances from Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown and Governor of the Bank of England Governor Eddie George later this week.
It was the committee's first meeting since the May 1 election.
UK interest rates have been raised three times since the election, twice since the central bank was granted power to set rates independently. They currently stand at 6.75 percent.

But two of the other economists testifying said there was more chance the Bank would undershoot its 2.5 inflation target by more than one percentage point than overshoot it to the same degree. Missing the target by one percent would require the Bank to send the Chancellor an open letter explaining itself.

Martin Weale, director of the National Institute of Economic and Social Research, said the government would have to treat the open 'excuse' letters carefully in order to avoid excessive interest rate rises and cuts.
"There is a danger of more erratic moves in the business cycle unless Brown takes a tolerent view of the letters he will regularly receive (from the Bank)."

He, along with Bill Martin, co-director of economic research at UBS, said there was a significant risk of a 'hard landing' for the economy. Weale forecast a 25 percent chance of a recession next year.

Martin said monetary policy mistakes made by the previous govnerment -- in particular a rate cut in December 1995 -- along with the cash rich corporate and household sectors, both of which have abnormally high savings levels, meant there was a good chance of an overheating, requiring a severe recession to cool it down.
"We might be into overheating territory already and a recession is inevitable and required," he said.
The fourth economist was Roger Bootle, chief group economist at HSBC.
